summary: Robotics data capture tooling, Full-stack engineering role, device-to-training-cluster pipelines plus labelling, search and QA internal tools

motivation_letter.name: Goonja Gandhi
paragraphs: Revel's brief reads less like four separate tools than one continuous problem: data leaves a device — vision, voice, motion — and has to arrive at a training cluster in a state someone can actually trust. Capture dashboards, live overlays, labelling, search and QA are the layers that decide whether it does. What interests me is that this cannot be solved by a frontend team handing work to a backend team; the failures that matter sit between the layers, and they stay invisible unless someone is willing to follow a single piece of data from the render loop to the socket. That is the kind of work I have been deliberately moving towards.

My habit as an engineer is to look one level beneath whatever I am building on. Wanting to understand how requests actually behave, I implemented HTTP myself on top of Node's net module, which meant working directly with TCP; I wrote a DNS resolver and spent time with streams, buffers and event-driven architecture. That work was deliberate study rather than production responsibility, but it changed how I debug: I am less interested in where a symptom appears than in which layer produces it. The instinct predates software — I studied linguistic philosophy before I wrote any, and the habit of asking what problem a concept is really solving transfers almost unchanged to protocols and abstractions.

Professionally, five years of frontend work — most of it at Tata Consultancy Services, where I also led a small team — covers the interface half of this role. The discipline that matters there is control over rendering and data flow rather than visual polish: a 68% reduction in bundle size, a Lighthouse score raised from 73 to 95, 40% fewer API calls through RxJS, and zero accessibility violations at QA. I mention the last one because a labelling tool used for hours a day is a working instrument, not a website. The backend half I have extended deliberately: Node, Express, GraphQL and REST in professional work, and in personal projects a semantic search system built on FAISS vector retrieval with LLM reasoning, where the lesson was that retrieval is not reasoning — search over captured data is precisely that problem. A later project used SSE streaming and the Web Speech API, which is closer to how a live overlay behaves: the interface has to stay useful while the data is still arriving.

I have not worked with robotic hardware, and I would rather say so plainly than leave it to be inferred. The hardware-specific parts of this role are what I would grow into; the surrounding work — reliable data movement, live visualisation, and tooling that makes a dataset inspectable — is where I have built depth. What attracts me is the end-to-end ownership: being the person who can follow a frame from a device, through the pipeline, into the interface where someone labels it, and notice when the two ends disagree about what the data means. I would like to build that kind of tooling at Revel.
motivation_letter.closing: Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to the opportunity to discuss how I can contribute.

summary: Consumer social platform, Software Engineer Web TypeScript role, event-driven growth and distribution systems

motivation_letter.name: Goonja Gandhi
paragraphs: Growth work is usually handed to a web engineer as another event in an analytics SDK. Amo describes it differently: growth levers, distribution flows, retention tracking and segmentation treated as systems to be architected, with durable event-driven workflows rather than campaign tooling. The smaller detail is the one that made me want to write this letter — invite pages with rich OG metadata. The first reader of that page is not a person but another platform's crawler, and it only performs if the rendering, metadata and caching decisions behind it are correct. The delivery layer is the growth mechanism, and that is the part of web engineering I have spent most of my career close to.

Over five years I have worked mostly on the rendered side of applications: Next.js App Router, SSR/SSG/ISR, React Server Components, SEO and Core Web Vitals, alongside the caching and code-splitting work that decides whether any of it holds up under real traffic. At TCS I led a team of five and reduced API calls by 40% through more deliberate RxJS state handling. More recently I built NewsAlign, an AI fact-verification platform, where I brought the bundle from 941KB to under 300KB and the Lighthouse score from 73 to 95, and where the backend constraints — caching, rate limiting, authentication, cost per query — turned out to matter as much as the interface.

That habit of looking underneath an API is the thread running through how I work. I wrote a small reactive engine modelled on React's useState internals mainly to see what happens between a state change and a repaint, and I have deliberately spent time below the application layer — Node.js streams, event-driven patterns, HTTP and TCP — to understand where durability and back-pressure are actually handled. It is why a Restate-based workflow interests me more than a typical frontend brief: correctness there is about retries, idempotency and state, not about pixels. I should be direct about the boundary: my production experience is largely web and application layer, and segmentation, lifecycle automation and monitoring are where I want to develop next rather than things I would claim to have done at scale. Internal dashboards and backoffice tooling appeal to me for the same underlying reason — their users make operational decisions, so accuracy and clarity matter more than surface.

What I would bring is ownership of the parts I have already done well: architecture and implementation of web systems, performance work measured against concrete targets, end-to-end delivery, code review and mentoring, and a habit of asking what problem a piece of infrastructure is solving before adding to it. I would like to work somewhere that treats growth and internal tooling as core engineering rather than afterthoughts, and this role reads like exactly that.
motivation_letter.closing: Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to the opportunity to discuss how I can contribute.

summary: Conversational AI sales agents, Full-Stack Product Engineer role, React/FastAPI/LLM/AWS product delivery

motivation_letter.name: Goonja Gandhi
paragraphs: Most AI demo tools treat the demo as a conversation problem. Karumi treats it as a grounding problem. A Karumi agent only works if it is fluent and simultaneously faithful to the material it was given — the product URL, the messaging document, the objection playbook — and if the conversation ends in something structured: a transcript, an analysis, and next steps already sitting in the CRM. A fluent interface that must stay correct about someone else's product, and that converts an open-ended conversation into a usable record, is the part of your product I keep returning to.

I worked on a similar shape of problem from the opposite direction when I built JobFinder. A rigid application form became a ten-question conversational interview, with OpenAI asking clarifying questions and the answers converted into a structured, reviewable profile, streamed to the client over SSE so the exchange felt immediate rather than batched. The hard part was not the prompt; it was keeping interview logic, AI integration, streaming, and profile extraction separable, so that a weak model response could not corrupt the structure underneath it. An earlier project, NewsAlign, taught me a related distinction: retrieval is not reasoning. A system that retrieves the right passages and then reasons explicitly over them behaves very differently from one that lets a fluent model improvise. For a demo agent, improvisation is precisely the failure mode — a confident, wrong claim about a customer's own product is worse than a demo that declines to answer.

That product also makes unusual frontend demands. The agent has to run inside someone else's landing page, application, or outbound email, which means it must load quickly, hold multi-turn and multilingual session state without drifting, and stay invisible to the host page's performance budget. This is the work I have done for five years. At TCS I led five developers on enterprise TypeScript applications and cut API calls by 40% through RxJS state handling; at Datapret I raised WCAG compliance by 30% on an accessibility-focused platform; on NewsAlign I reduced the bundle from 941KB to under 300KB and moved Lighthouse performance from 73 to 95. I also built a small reactive state engine to understand what useState actually does underneath the API — a habit that matters when an embeddable agent UI becomes state-heavy.

Because transcripts and CRM records hold what prospects say about their own problems, the GDPR, SOC 2, and ISO 27001 posture you list is not paperwork; it shapes how conversations are stored, replayed, and retained. I would want to work at the boundary where the embeddable client meets the grounding and logging layer, where a small team's decisions about streaming, caching, cost, and data retention actually get made. That kind of end-to-end ownership is what I am looking for, and I would bring frontend depth alongside a deliberate, still-developing understanding of the systems beneath it.
motivation_letter.closing: Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to the opportunity to discuss how I can contribute.
